newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong shares retreat, Tokyo also weaker.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong shares retreat, Tokyo also weaker.

text.p: Hong Kong stocks retreated on Thursday, breaking a record-setting rally, and Tokyo's key Nikkei index also slipped, pressured by profit-taking.

Most Asian markets closed weaker. Bangkok suffered the heaviest losses, shedding 1.15 percent from its benchmark index as uncertainty continued over the new government's key economic cabinet appointments.
Brokers said resistance at 13,200 points broke the Hong Kong Hang Seng index's three-day run of record closes. The index ended 67.60 points or 0.51 percent lower at 13,099.56.
The index earlier set a record intra-day high of 13,237.73.
Turnover was HK$10.68 billion compared with HK$12.29 billion on Wednesday.
"It needs to correct. It wants to correct," said Miles Remington, sales trader at Crosby Securities.
"It hit technical resistance at 13,200...I think we possihly are going to find it difficult to get through there," he said.
Fears of share placements by blue chip companies also prompted some investors to take profits. Despite Thursday's loss, the Hang Seng index has risen 210.19 points this week.

Tokyo's key Nikkei 225 finished at 21,143.34, down 46.62 points or 0.22 percent after clawing up as high as 21,301.26. The index's earlier gains, driven by strong demand for blue-chip issues, were eroded by profit-taking, brokers said.
News that Japan's Ministry of Finance ordered Hanwa Bank to stop most operations had little impact on trade.
"The overseas markets didn't panic on hearing the Hanwa failure news so that helped the Tokyo stock market keep its cool," Akihiro Naemura, strategist at Okasan Securities, said.
In pre-market hours, the Finance Ministry suspended most business activities of the bank sagging under the weight of 190 billion yen in problem loans.
Thai share prices closed sharply lower at 955.35, down 11.08 points, or 1.15 percent.
Brokers said sentiment continued to soften as negotiations between coalition partners over key economic cabinet appointments showed no signs of progress.
Bombay's market also sagged, hurt by an onslaught of disappointing first-half company results.
The 30-share BSE index slid 0.72 percent, or 22.12 points to finish at a provisional 3040.38.
Taiwan's brief bull run came to a halt as stocks were hit by profit-taking after a dramatic recent rise and by shock at the gangland-style executions of six people in a Taiwan official's home.
At the close, the index had fallen 36.87 points or 0.55 percent at 6,692.98. Turnover was an active T$83.8 billion.

Brokers warned the killings would rekindle concerns about Taiwan's poor social order and could chill market sentiment. But they added investors used the shooting as an excuse to take profits following the market's close at a 22-month high on Wednesday.
Jakarta's Composite index fell 3.77 points, or 0.62 percent, to close at 602.99 points, dragged down by losses in market heavyweight Telkom, brokers said.
Profit-taking dented Manila blue chip shares, brokers said, pulling the main index into negative territory.
The index finished 18.51 points lower, or 0.59 percent, at 3,099.11.
Australian stocks were also deflated by profit-takers, who burst a record-breaking bubble formed in the morning session.
Inspired by Wall Street's run of record finishes, the key index vaulted over the 2,400 point barrier early. But its peak of 2,406.2 tempted profit-takers into the market.
At the close, the All Ordinaries index was 0.2 points lower at 2,392.5, barely changed from Wednesday's close.
Singapore shares managed to gain ground, helped by strong interest in property stocks, dealers said.
The STII closed up 3.41 points or 0.16 percent, at 2,197.69.
At 11.15 GMT, the dollar traded at 111.61/1.71 yen and 1.4970/77 marks.
Hong Kong gold prices sank to end at $377.85/378.35 an ounce against Wednesday's New York close of $378.20/80.
SIMEX Brent crude futures jumped, the prompt January contract last trading at $22.80 per barrel, up 26 cents from London's close.
